newsitem.title: ITALY: Separatist Bossi blasts Italy, plans own "militia". [CORRECTED 15/9 09:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Separatist Bossi blasts Italy, plans own "militia". [CORRECTED 15/9 09:30 GMT]

text.p: Separatist leader Umberto Bossi on Saturday accused Italy in the wake of a bomb attack of firing the first shot in a battle with his self-styled northern state and said he was planning to set up his own militia force.

In a rambling speech in the town of Boretto in his Northern League party homeland of Lombardy, Bossi told several thousand supporters that he had learnt of an overnight bomb attack against party offices in Venice (Corrects from Verona).

"Italy threw the bomb first," Bossi declared on the banks of the River Po, where he has been staging a cross-Italy "March to the Sea" due to culminate on Sunday in Venice with a declaration of independence for his would-be "Padania".
The attack, which police were investigating, was caused by a home-made bomb. Damage was slight.

"I hope that the first act of the provisional government will be to pass as soon as possible a decree for the voluntary enrolment in the Padanian National Guard...the old Roman trickery won't work any more," the fiery leader added.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi has dismissed Bossi's secessionist campaign as "a ridiculous game".
Bossi's party won a surprising 10.6 percent in a general election in April but a new opinion poll showed only 7.6 percent of Italians favoured secession and 85.6 percent were opposed.
Bossi already has a green-shirted band of volunteers making up the League's security detachment, plus a self-styled parliament of the north and its own would-be government.

Magistrates in Turin said on Saturday they were conducting formal investigations into Bossi's secessionist proposals and the role of the "green shirts" following denunciations by individual citizens and a southern Italian group.
Bossi, wearing a green, scout-style neckchief, commented on the increased police presence, comparing it with an earlier rally in Cremona. Bossi said it was proof Rome was scared.

No trouble was reported, however -- a welcome relief after ugly scenes at the close of the first day on Friday when far-left youths pelted League supporters with stones and glass, injuring about 12 people including police officers. Police used tear gas to disperse the clash but no one was seriously hurt.

Nevertheless, police were on alert for Sunday's first division soccer match between Atalanta and Florence in the northern town of Bergamo after Atalanta fans sent an anonymous letter to the rival club threatening violence.
"Do not return to Bergamo, lest it become your grave," said the letter, postmarked "Bergamo, Padania". Fans from the two sides clashed during the Italian Cup final last May.

As in the earlier event, the far-right National Alliance party flew a plane overhead trailing a banner proclaiming "Viva L'Italia". Leader Gianfranco Fini, who plans a pro-unity rally in Milan on Sunday, declared Bossi's campaign "a flop".

Another anti-Bossi rally, a concert attended by Italian pop singer Luca Barbarossa, began on Saturday evening in the mediaeval town of Mantua, the seat of Bossi's self-styled parliament, and was due to go on all night.

Bossi himself was taken by car -- with Rome registration plates -- back to the catamaran in which he sailed from Cremona for his onward journey to Borgoforte, 12 km (7.5 miles) from Mantua, for his final rally of the day.
Party officials said they expected 70,000 people to attend their "party" in favour of splitting Italy's richest region off from the poor, agricultural south.

Bossi earlier slammed the media, saying they lived "in their own virtual world where they invent any old rubbish". He accused them of lying about attendance at events on Friday, which began when he symbolically filled a flask with water from the source of the Po to symbolise the birth of his nation.

Bossi's grand finale was due on Sunday evening when he promised that millions of supporters would flock to Venice for the ritual proclamation. The League has drawn a parallel with the U.S. declaration of independence in 1776.
Earlier in the day, the League plans to stage a ritual burning of fake RAI television licence papers.
